title: This road map could help us decide whether to deploy solar geoengineering
gist: San Francisco nonprofit Reflective has published a detailed, costed, multi-decade research road map for stratospheric aerosol injection (solar geoengineering) — estimated at $370 million over roughly a decade if coordinated, or $1.4 billion over 20 years if not — laying out staged outdoor experiments with built-in 'stop' gates, while critics argue the deepest questions (who controls and deploys a planet-altering technology, and the risk of abrupt 'termination shock') are governance issues no amount of research can resolve.

themes.theme: The road map: cost, timeline, and staging

insights.claim: Reflective's SAI Research Roadmap estimates that a fully coordinated global research effort to resolve key scientific uncertainties about stratospheric aerosol injection would take about a decade and cost around $370 million, versus roughly 20 years and nearly $1.4 billion if research remains uncoordinated.
insights.speaker: James Temple
insights.so_what: Puts a concrete price tag and timeline on de-risking a planet-scale climate intervention technology — a benchmark for philanthropic/government funders evaluating geoengineering research allocation versus other climate spending.
insights.quote: If all the work is done in a coordinated way, it would take about a decade and cost around $370 million—and if it's not, it would require roughly 20 years and nearly $1.4 billion

insights.claim: The road map's first phase ('foundational knowledge') would run two to three years and cost $30-75 million on computer simulations, lab experiments, and observational tooling; the second phase would release small doses (10 metric tons of sulfur dioxide, four times over two seasons) via modified aircraft over four to eight years and $70-150 million, cutting uncertainty about solar geoengineering's cooling efficacy by roughly 25%.
insights.speaker: James Temple
insights.so_what: Gives investors/funders a granular, staged budget and expected uncertainty-reduction metric (25% efficacy-uncertainty reduction from ~$150M of phase-two spend) to evaluate cost-effectiveness of early-stage geoengineering research funding.
insights.quote: The full research stage could take four to eight years and cost $70 million to $150 million, the report says. The work during it may reduce uncertainty about the 'cooling efficacy' of solar geoengineering... by about 25%.
insights.locator: The next stage would include using modified aircraft

insights.claim: A later, larger-scale road map phase would release 25,000 tons of sulfur dioxide over one season (at least once, possibly twice), running four to eleven years and costing $270 million to $1.1 billion, and would cut efficacy uncertainty by around 66% — followed by a final phase of ongoing monitoring only if the world actually deploys solar geoengineering at full scale.
insights.speaker: James Temple
insights.so_what: The bulk of uncertainty reduction (66%) is concentrated in the most expensive and most controversial phase ($270M-$1.1B, 25,000-ton releases) — the real decision bottleneck for funders and regulators will be authorizing this specific stage, not the earlier lab/small-scale work.
insights.quote: That research stage, which includes other work as well, would last four to 11 years, run $270 million to $1.1 billion, and decrease efficacy uncertainty by around 66%, according to the road map.
insights.locator: The experiments during the next phase

insights.claim: Reflective has deliberately built 'stage gates' into the road map between later research phases, meaning research is designed to halt if experiments show the intervention lacks the hoped-for cooling impact, reveals worrisome downsides, or fails to resolve key uncertainties.
insights.speaker: Dakota Gruener
insights.so_what: A pre-committed stop-gate design is a governance mechanism that could make outdoor geoengineering experiments more politically palatable to skeptical regulators/publics than an open-ended research program — worth watching whether funders/governments adopt this staged-gate model as a template for other high-risk climate tech.
insights.quote: Our road map has these gates precisely because there may be points where the answer is 'You should stop.'

insights.claim: Reflective, incorporated in late 2023 by CEO Dakota Gruener, has raised more than $20 million from prominent charities and individuals and has distributed around $4 million of that to several dozen external research groups studying solar geoengineering, alongside building its own open-source solar geoengineering simulator and an SAI Uncertainties database.
insights.speaker: James Temple
insights.so_what: Reflective has become a de facto funding and coordination hub for solar geoengineering research in under three years — a named institution to track for future grant announcements, database updates, and its influence on how this research field gets prioritized.
insights.quote: It has now raised more than $20 million from a number of prominent charities and individuals, and it's provided around $4 million to several dozen research groups.
insights.locator: Since Gruener incorporated Reflective in late 2023

insights.claim: The UK's Advanced Research and Invention Agency (ARIA) funded 21 separate geoengineering research projects last year, indicating that government-level funding momentum for this field already extends beyond Reflective's own philanthropic model.
insights.speaker: James Temple
insights.so_what: A UK government research agency actively co-funding 21 geoengineering projects signals the field is moving from purely academic/philanthropic funding toward state-backed programs — a jurisdiction (UK) to watch for policy and funding signals ahead of the US or other governments.
insights.quote: Ilan Gur, the former CEO of the Advanced Research and Invention Agency (ARIA), the UK research department that funded 21 geoengineering research projects last year, applauds Reflective's road map.

themes.theme: The governance objection: research can't answer 'who decides'

insights.claim: Aarti Gupta, co-initiator of an international non-use agreement campaign, argues the central questions around stratospheric aerosol injection are not technical but about control: who would develop and deploy a planet-altering technology, to serve whose purposes, given that it will inevitably create winners and losers.
insights.speaker: Aarti Gupta
insights.so_what: A framework investors/policymakers should apply to any geoengineering research proposal: technical uncertainty reduction (Reflective's stated goal) does not resolve the separate, arguably harder question of legitimate global governance and distributional impact — expect this objection to keep surfacing as a blocker regardless of research progress.
insights.quote: The core question is: Who would control a planet-altering technology like stratospheric aerosol injection? Who would develop it, and who would deploy it, and to what end?

insights.claim: Since 2002, hundreds of academics have signed an open letter calling for a ban on outdoor solar geoengineering experiments and an 'international non-use agreement,' arguing the technology could never be governed in a globally equitable way — a sustained, organized opposition movement predating Reflective's road map by decades.
insights.speaker: James Temple
insights.so_what: Organized scientific opposition to outdoor SAI testing is long-standing and broad (hundreds of signatories), not a fringe reaction to this specific road map — a durable political headwind for any funder or government considering backing Reflective's proposed experiments.
insights.quote: Since 2002, hundreds of academics have signed an open letter calling for a ban on outdoor experiments and an "international non-use agreement,"

insights.claim: Two prior real-world attempts at outdoor solar geoengineering experiments — Harvard's SCoPEx and the UK-based SPICE project — were ultimately halted amid opposition from environmentalists or policymakers, showing that political/social resistance, not just funding or technical readiness, has been the binding constraint on this research to date.
insights.speaker: James Temple
insights.so_what: A track record of two high-profile project cancellations under public/political pressure is a concrete base rate for the probability that Reflective's proposed larger outdoor experiments also get blocked, independent of their scientific merit or funding.
insights.quote: Several earlier proposals to carry out such experiments, including Harvard's SCoPEx and the UK-based SPICE project, were ultimately halted amid opposition from environmentalists or policymakers.

insights.claim: Legal scholar Wil Burns argues that once solar geoengineering is deployed to mask continued greenhouse gas warming, future generations who had no say in the decision could not safely turn it off without triggering 'termination shock' — a sudden surge of previously masked warming — making full-scale deployment intergenerationally unjustifiable regardless of how much research is done.
insights.speaker: Wil Burns
insights.so_what: Termination shock is the key tail-risk mechanism that makes solar geoengineering fundamentally different from a reversible technology investment: once deployed at scale, walking it back has its own catastrophic risk, creating a lock-in dynamic worth flagging in any long-horizon climate risk model.
insights.quote: What that would do, in my mind, is put a sword of Damocles over future generations. So even if you could, quote-unquote, 'prove it works,' I don't think from an intergenerational perspective it would ever be tenable.

themes.theme: Risk framing and counter-arguments for proceeding

insights.claim: Reflective CEO Dakota Gruener frames the alternative to funded, staged research not as 'no deployment ever happening,' but as decisions on solar geoengineering being made 'in a panic or on lack of evidence' as climate pressure mounts — reframing the choice as research-now versus improvised-crisis-response-later, rather than research-versus-never.
insights.speaker: Dakota Gruener
insights.so_what: This framing is the core strategic argument Reflective is using to win over cautious funders and policymakers — expect it to be echoed in future fundraising and advocacy messaging as climate impacts intensify and pressure to 'do something' grows.
insights.quote: We don't think the alternative is decisions not happening at all. We think the alternative is decisions being made in a panic or on lack of evidence.

insights.claim: Gruener notes that the proposed initial outdoor experiment — releasing 10 tons of sulfur dioxide — amounts to less than 2% of what the global aviation industry already releases into the atmosphere each day, a comparison used to argue the early-stage experimental risk is minimal.
insights.speaker: Dakota Gruener
insights.so_what: A concrete comparative benchmark (vs. daily global aviation SO2 output) that proponents will use to counter 'dangerous experiment' framing in public and regulatory debate — useful for assessing whether opposition to Phase 2 specifically is proportionate to its actual physical footprint.
insights.quote: She notes that 10 tons of sulfur dioxide is less than 2% of the amount that the global aviation industry releases into the atmosphere each day.

insights.claim: Sebastian Eastham, an Imperial College London researcher on an ARIA-funded cooling project, argues that relying solely on computer simulations without ever conducting outdoor experiments risks researchers 'spinning their wheels' rerunning the same models without learning essential things about solar geoengineering's real-world effectiveness or dangers.
insights.speaker: Sebastian Eastham
insights.so_what: A working-scientist counter to the no-outdoor-experiments position: pure simulation has diminishing returns, so the debate isn't simulation-vs-field-test in the abstract but how much field testing is justified — relevant for evaluating competing research-methodology claims in the SAI funding debate.
